Or it is rather to be understood of the armies of the Romans, which were abominable to the Jews (they could not endure them), which <hi type="italic">overspread the nation,</hi> and by which it was <hi type="italic">made desolate;</hi> for these are the words which Christ refers to, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.15">Matt. xxiv. 15</reference>, <hi type="italic">When you shall see the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel, stand in the holy place, then let those who shall be in Judea flee,</hi> which is explained <reference osisRef="Luke.21.20">Luke xxi. 20</reference>, <hi type="italic">When you shall see Jerusalem encompassed with armies then flee.</hi> [7.] That the desolation shall be total and final: <hi type="italic">He shall make it desolate, even until the consummation,</hi> that is, he shall make it completely desolate. It is a <hi type="italic">desolation determined,</hi> and it will be accomplished to the utmost. And when it is made desolate, it should seem, there is something more determined that is to be <hi type="italic">poured upon the desolate</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.27">v. 27</reference>), and what should that be but the <hi type="italic">spirit of slumber</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.8">Rom. xi. 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.25">25</reference>), that blindness which has happened to Israel until the fulness of the Gentiles shall come in? And <hi type="italic">then all Israel shall be saved.</hi>  <chapter eID="Dan.9"/> <div eID="gen19572" type="x-p"/>

entries.11dd8c38f674c05247ea1edd3a26ccfae8baa644: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12137"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 9</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Dan.9.1-Dan.9.27">Da 9:1-27</reference>. Daniel's Confession and Prayer for Jerusalem: Gabriel Comforts Him by the Prophecy of the Seventy Weeks.</title> <div sID="gen21983" type="x-p"/> The world powers here recede from view; Israel, and the salvation by Messiah promised to it, are the subject of revelation. Israel had naturally expected salvation at the end of the captivity. Daniel is therefore told, that, after the seventy years of the captivity, seventy times seven must elapse, and that even then Messiah would not come in glory as the Jews might through misunderstanding expect from the earlier prophets, but by dying would put away sin. This ninth chapter (Messianic prophecy) stands between the two visions of the Old Testament Antichrist, to comfort "the wise." In the interval between Antiochus and Christ, no further revelation was needed; therefore, as in the first part of the book, so in the second, Christ and Antichrist in connection are the theme.<div eID="gen21983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21984" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12137"/><hi type="bold">1. first year of Darius--</hi>Cyaxares II, in whose name Cyrus, his nephew, son-in-law, and successor, took Babylon, 538 B.C. The date of this chapter is therefore 537 B.C., a year before Cyrus permitted the Jews to return from exile, and sixty-nine years after Daniel had been carried captive at the beginning of the captivity, 606 B.C.<div eID="gen21984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21985" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">son of Ahasuerus--</hi>called Astyages by Xenophon. Ahasuerus was a name common to many of the kings of Medo-Persia.<div eID="gen21985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21986" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">made king--</hi>The phrase implies that Darius owed the kingdom not to his own prowess, but to that of another, namely, Cyrus. <div eID="gen21986" type="x-p"/>
entries.4c21c1592f1ac37b964843cde81685a44e642952: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12138"/><div sID="gen21987" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12138"/><hi type="bold">2. understood by books--</hi>rather, "letters," that is, Jeremiah's letter (<reference osisRef="Jer.29.10">Jr 29:10</reference>) to the captives in Babylon; also <reference osisRef="Jer.25.11">Jr 25:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.12">12</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.21">2Ch 36:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.30.18">Jr 30:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.31.38">31:38</reference>. God's promises are the ground on which we should, like Daniel, rest sure hope; not so as to make our prayers needless, but rather to encourage them. <div eID="gen21987" type="x-p"/>
entries.d04a69f9877ad8694a1b3a37b1af5cc3c76d31a9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12139"/><div sID="gen21988" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12139"/><hi type="bold">3. prayer ... supplications--</hi>literally, "intercessions ... entreaties for mercy." Praying for blessings, and deprecating evils. <div eID="gen21988" type="x-p"/>
entries.00a8a126d5f0d6a1b87513513199a86ac20ecf6a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12140"/><div sID="gen21989" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12140"/><hi type="bold">4. my confession--</hi>according to God's promises in <reference osisRef="Lev.26.39-Lev.26.42">Le 26:39-42</reference>, that if Israel in exile for sin should repent and confess, God would remember for them His covenant with Abraham (compare <reference osisRef="Deut.30.1-Deut.30.5">De 30:1-5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.29.12-Jer.29.14">Jr 29:12-14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.4.10">Jas 4:10</reference>). God's promise was absolute, but prayer also was ordained as about to precede its fulfilment, this too being the work of God in His people, as much as the external restoration which was to follow. So it shall be at Israel's final restoration (<reference osisRef="Ps.102.13-Ps.102.17">Psa 102:13-17</reference>). Daniel takes his countrymen's place of confession of sin, identifying himself with them, and, as their representative and intercessory priest, "accepts the punishment of their iniquity." Thus he typifies Messiah, the Sin-bearer and great Intercessor. The prophet's own life and experience form the fit starting point of the prophecy concerning the sin atonement. He prays for Israel's restoration as associated in the prophets (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.31.4">Jr 31:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.11.12">11, 12</reference>, 31, &c.) with the hope of Messiah. The revelation, now granted, analyzes into its successive parts that which the prophets, in prophetical perspective, heretofore saw together in one; namely, the redemption from captivity, and the full Messianic redemption. God's servants, who, like Noah's father (<reference osisRef="Gen.5.29">Ge 5:29</reference>), hoped many a time that now the Comforter of their afflictions was at hand, had to wait from age to age, and to view preceding fulfilments only as pledges of the coming of Him whom they so earnestly desired to see (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.17">Mt 13:17</reference>); as now also Christians, who believe that the Lord's second coming is nigh, are expected to continue waiting. So Daniel is informed of a long period of seventy prophetic weeks before Messiah's coming, instead of seventy years, as he might have expected (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.18.21">Mt 18:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.18.22">22</reference>) [Auberlen].<div eID="gen21989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21990" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">great and dreadful God--</hi>as we know to our cost by the calamities we suffer. The greatness of God and His dreadful abhorrence of sin should prepare sinners for reverent, humble acknowledgment of the justice of their punishment.<div eID="gen21990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21991" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">keeping ... covenant and mercy--</hi>that is, the covenant of Thy mercy, whereby Thou hast promised to deliver us, not for our merits, but of Thy mercy (<reference osisRef="Ezek.36.22">Eze 36:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.23">23</reference>). So weak and sinful is man that any covenant for good on God's part with him, to take effect, must depend solely on His grace. If He be a God to be feared for His justice, He is one to be trusted for His "mercy."<div eID="gen21991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21992" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">love ... keep his commandments--</hi>Keeping His commandments is the only sure test of love to God (<reference osisRef="John.14.15">Joh 14:15</reference>). <div eID="gen21992" type="x-p"/>
entries.c8c45f3e1c43d7b0aca03f8870382cb716331de5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12141"/><div sID="gen21993" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12141"/>5. Compare Nehemiah's confession (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.1-Neh.9.38">Ne 9:1-38</reference>).<div eID="gen21993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21994" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sinned ... committed iniquity ... done wickedly ... rebelled--</hi>a climax. Erred in ignorance ... sinned by infirmity ... habitually and wilfully done wickedness ... as open and obstinate rebels set ourselves against God. <div eID="gen21994" type="x-p"/>
entries.0a3a9ece4934bef1c22dbc2e814b76433a8622d6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12142"/><div sID="gen21995" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12142"/><hi type="bold">6. prophets ... spake ... to our kings ... to all the people--</hi>They fearlessly warned all without respect of persons. <div eID="gen21995" type="x-p"/>
entries.75c5bf6ac0534df32e63a85918a2860e66ab9ce6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12143"/><div sID="gen21996" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12143"/><hi type="bold">7. confusion of faces, as at this day--</hi>Shame at our guilt, betrayed in our countenance, is what belongs to us; as our punishment "at this day" attests.<div eID="gen21996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21997" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">near, and ... far off--</hi>the chastisement, however varied, some Jews not being cast off so far from Jerusalem as others, all alike were sharers in the guilt. <div eID="gen21997" type="x-p"/>
entries.5eb4ca5a15c4be6bf1299353bef2c2b42226ebbb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12144"/><div sID="gen21998" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12144"/><hi type="bold">9. mercies--</hi>The plural intensifies the force; mercy manifold and exhibited in countless ways. As it is humbling to recollect "righteousness belongeth unto God," so it is comforting, that "mercies belong to the Lord OUR God."<div eID="gen21998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21999" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">though we have rebelled--</hi>rather, "since," &c. [Vulgate], (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.11">Psa 25:11</reference>). Our punishment is not inconsistent with His "mercies," since we have rebelled against Him. <div eID="gen21999" type="x-p"/>
entries.719fd0b20be9be6661031a2e6bc10a5d71f0ae03: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12145"/><div sID="gen22000" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12145"/><hi type="bold">10. set before us--</hi>not ambiguously, but plainly, so that we were without excuse. <div eID="gen22000" type="x-p"/>
entries.7aefdf23a8ff4378ee93b57376834d8b3d7b0eb1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12146"/><div sID="gen22001" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12146"/><hi type="bold">11. all--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.14.3">Psa 14:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.3.12">Ro 3:12</reference>).<div eID="gen22001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22002" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the curse ... and ... oath ... in ... law--</hi>the curse against Israel, if disobedient, which God ratified by oath (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.14-Lev.26.39">Le 26:14-39</reference>; De 27:15-26; 28:15-68; <reference osisRef="Deut.29.1-Deut.29.29">29:1-29</reference>). <div eID="gen22002" type="x-p"/>
entries.0609d27633d01f9bd28e04bbd3b5238489873fa9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12147"/><div sID="gen22003" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12147"/><hi type="bold">12. confirmed his words--</hi>showed by the punishments we suffer, that His words were no idle threats.<div eID="gen22003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22004" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">under ... heaven hath not been done as ... upon Jerusalem--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Lam.1.12">La 1:12</reference>). <div eID="gen22004" type="x-p"/>
entries.342eaabc8113cbedf81139c1bb3348303c48b216: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12148"/><div sID="gen22005" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12148"/><hi type="bold">13. yet made we not our prayer before--</hi>literally, "soothed not the face of." Not even our chastisement has taught us penitence (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.13">Is 9:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.5.3">Jr 5:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.7.10">Ho 7:10</reference>). Diseased, we spurn the healing medicine.<div eID="gen22005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22006" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that we might turn, &c.--</hi>Prayer can only be accepted when joined with the desire to turn from sin to God (<reference osisRef="Ps.66.18">Psa 66:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.28.9">Pr 28:9</reference>).<div eID="gen22006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22007" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">understand thy truth--</hi>"attentively regard Thy faithfulness" in fulfilling Thy promises, and also Thy threats [Calvin]. Thy law (<reference osisRef="Dan.8.12">Da 8:12</reference>), [Maurer]. <div eID="gen22007" type="x-p"/>
entries.93c298ba53b3561276f08ecfb6e656fa77e2c54c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12149"/><div sID="gen22008" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12149"/><hi type="bold">14. watched upon the evil--</hi>expressing ceaseless vigilance that His people's sins might not escape His judgment, as a watchman on guard night and day (<reference osisRef="Job.14.16">Job 14:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.31.28">Jr 31:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.44.27">44:27</reference>). God watching upon the Jews' punishment forms a striking contrast to the Jews' slumbering in their sins.<div eID="gen22008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22009" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">God is righteous--</hi>True penitents "justify" God, "ascribing righteousness to Him," instead of complaining of their punishment as too severe (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.33">Ne 9:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.36.3">Job 36:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.51.4">Psa 51:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.3.39-Lam.3.42">La 3:39-42</reference>). <div eID="gen22009" type="x-p"/>
entries.e54cda7684b1aa1772d2f081fe5b01e4418bdaa4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12150"/><div sID="gen22010" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12150"/><hi type="bold">15. brought thy people ... out of ... Egypt--</hi>a proof to all ages that the seed of Abraham is Thy covenant-people. That ancient benefit gives us hope that Thou wilt confer a like one on us now under similar circumstances (<reference osisRef="Ps.80.8-Ps.80.14">Psa 80:8-14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.32.21">Jr 32:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.23.7">23:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.23.8">8</reference>).<div eID="gen22010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22011" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as at this day--</hi>is known. <div eID="gen22011" type="x-p"/>
entries.439708fd67cfe0ecd58f0d9967a05a99e87e1b8e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12151"/><div sID="gen22012" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12151"/><hi type="bold">16. thy righteousness--</hi>not stern justice in punishing, but Thy faithfulness to Thy promises of mercy to them who trust in Thee (<reference osisRef="Ps.31.1">Psa 31:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.143.1">143:1</reference>).<div eID="gen22012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22013" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy city--</hi>chosen as Thine in the election of grace, which changes not.<div eID="gen22013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22014" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for ... iniquities of ... fathers--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Exod.20.5">Ex 20:5</reference>). He does not impugn God's justice in this, as did the murmurers (<reference osisRef="Ezek.18.2">Eze 18:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.18.3">3</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Jer.31.29">Jr 31:29</reference>).<div eID="gen22014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22015" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy people ... a reproach--</hi>which brings reproach on Thy name. "All the nations that are about us" will say that Thou, Jehovah, wast not able to save Thy peculiar people. So <reference osisRef="Dan.9.17">Da 9:17</reference>, "for the Lord's sake"; <reference osisRef="Dan.9.19">Da 9:19</reference>, "for Thine own sake" (<reference osisRef="Isa.48.9">Is 48:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.48.11">11</reference>). <div eID="gen22015" type="x-p"/>
entries.901fea5a9f6bca6745542d96dfacf120dbd2ede6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12152"/><div sID="gen22016" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12152"/><hi type="bold">17. cause thy face to shine--</hi>metaphor from the sun, which gladdens all that it beams upon (<reference osisRef="Num.6.25">Nu 6:25</reference>; Mal 4:2). <div eID="gen22016" type="x-p"/>
entries.fa3e66473c47c8844a501b0d7df5e750555b6089: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12153"/><div sID="gen22017" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12153"/><hi type="bold">18. present ... supplications--</hi>literally, "cause to fall," &c. (compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Jer.36.7">Jr 36:7</reference>). <div eID="gen22017" type="x-p"/>
entries.dcffacc7cc83b904c7e3935ca499f0bff2dab69c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12154"/><div sID="gen22018" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12154"/>19. The short broken ejaculations and repetitions show the intense fervor of his supplications.<div eID="gen22018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22019" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">defer not--</hi>He implies that the seventy years are now all but complete.<div eID="gen22019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22020" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thine own sake--</hi>often repeated, as being the strongest plea (<reference osisRef="Jer.14.21">Jr 14:21</reference>). <div eID="gen22020" type="x-p"/>
entries.a2e04f20c815da23721b472323cb5fa9d456db21: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12155"/><div sID="gen22021" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12155"/><hi type="bold">20. whiles I was speaking--</hi>repeated in <reference osisRef="Dan.9.21">Da 9:21</reference>; emphatically marking that the answer was given before the prayer was completed, as God promised (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.19">Is 30:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.65.24">65:24</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Ps.32.5">Psa 32:5</reference>). <div eID="gen22021" type="x-p"/>
entries.83d33e3133128908d1bac7a01e518e7c246c7bed: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12156"/><div sID="gen22022" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12156"/><hi type="bold">21. I had seen in the vision at the beginning--</hi>namely, in the former vision by the river Ulai (<reference osisRef="Dan.8.1">Da 8:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.8.16">16</reference>).<div eID="gen22022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22023" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fly swiftly--</hi>literally, "with weariness," that is, move swiftly as one breathless and wearied out with quick running [Gesenius]. English Version is better (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.2">Is 6:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.6">Eze 1:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.14.6">Re 14:6</reference>).<div eID="gen22023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22024" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">time of ... evening oblation--</hi>the ninth hour, three o'clock (compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.36">1Ki 18:36</reference>). As formerly, when the temple stood, this hour was devoted to sacrifices, so now to prayer. Daniel, during the whole captivity to the very last, with pious patriotism never forgot God's temple-worship, but speaks of its rites long abolished, as if still in use. <div eID="gen22024" type="x-p"/>
entries.9be255def732ae03500c4d8574b104fe6c5bafaf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12157"/><div sID="gen22025" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12157"/><hi type="bold">22. to give thee ... understanding--</hi><reference osisRef="Dan.8.16">Da 8:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.8.26">Da 8:26</reference> shows that the symbolical vision had not been understood. God therefore now gives "information" directly, instead of by symbol, which required interpretation. <div eID="gen22025" type="x-p"/>
entries.f6b0bef7babcadd653d2cf359677537512af28b6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12158"/><div sID="gen22026" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12158"/><hi type="bold">23. At the beginning of thy supplications, &c.--</hi>The promulgation of the divine decree was made in heaven to the angels as soon as Daniel began to pray.<div eID="gen22026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22027" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">came forth--</hi>from the divine throne; so <reference osisRef="Dan.9.22">Da 9:22</reference>.<div eID="gen22027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22028" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou art greatly beloved--</hi>literally, "a man of desires" (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.6">Eze 23:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.12">12</reference>); the object of God's delight. As the apocalyptic prophet of the New Testament was "the disciple whom Jesus loved," so the apocalyptic prophet of the Old Testament was "greatly beloved" of God.<div eID="gen22028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22029" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the vision--</hi>the further revelation as to Messiah in connection with Jeremiah's prophecy of seventy years of the captivity. The charge to "understand" is the same as in <reference osisRef="Matt.24.15">Mt 24:15</reference>, where Rome primarily, and Antichrist ultimately, is referred to (compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Dan.9.27">Da 9:27</reference>). <div eID="gen22029" type="x-p"/>
entries.455e43f8a86fe0770e308f28cda17b26078e6070: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12159"/><div sID="gen22030" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12159"/><hi type="bold">24. Seventy weeks--</hi>namely, of years; literally, "Seventy sevens"; seventy heptads or hebdomads; four hundred ninety years; expressed in a form of "concealed definiteness" [Hengstenberg], a usual way with the prophets. The Babylonian captivity is a turning point in the history of the kingdom of God. It terminated the free Old Testament theocracy. Up to that time Israel, though oppressed at times, was; as a rule, free. From the Babylonian captivity the theocracy never recovered its full freedom down to its entire suspension by Rome; and this period of Israel's subjection to the Gentiles is to continue till the millennium (<reference osisRef="Rev.20.1-Rev.20.15">Re 20:1-15</reference>), when Israel shall be restored as head of the New Testament theocracy, which will embrace the whole earth. The free theocracy ceased in the first year of Nebuchadnezzar, and the fourth of Jehoiakim; the year of the world 3338, the point at which the seventy years of the captivity begin. Heretofore Israel had a right, if subjugated by a foreign king, to shake off the yoke (<reference osisRef="Judg.4.1-Judg.5.31">Jud 4:1-5:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.7">2Ki 18:7</reference>) as an unlawful one, at the first opportunity. But the prophets (<reference osisRef="Jer.27.9-Jer.27.11">Jr 27:9-11</reference>) declared it to be God's will that they should submit to Babylon. Hence every effort of Jehoiakim, Jeconiah, and Zedekiah to rebel was vain. The period of the world times, and of Israel's depression, from the Babylonian captivity to the millennium, though abounding more in afflictions (for example, the two destructions of Jerusalem, Antiochus' persecution, and those which Christians suffered), contains all that was good in the preceding ones, summed up in Christ, but in a way visible only to the eye of faith. Since He came as a servant, He chose for His appearing the period darkest of all as to His people's temporal state. Always fresh persecutors have been rising, whose end is destruction, and so it shall be with the last enemy, Antichrist. As the Davidic epoch is the point of the covenant-people's highest glory, so the captivity is that of their lowest humiliation. Accordingly, the people's sufferings are reflected in the picture of the suffering Messiah. He is no longer represented as the theocratic King, the Antitype of David, but as the Servant of God and Son of man; at the same time the cross being the way to glory (compare <reference osisRef="Dan.9.1-Dan.9.27">Da 9:1-27</reference> with <reference osisRef="Dan.2.34">Da 2:34</reference>, 35, 44; <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.7">12:7</reference>). In the second and seventh chapters, Christ's first coming is not noticed, for Daniel's object was to prophesy to his nation as to the whole period from the destruction to the re-establishment of Israel; but this ninth chapter minutely predicts Christ's first coming, and its effects on the covenant people. The seventy weeks date thirteen years before the rebuilding of Jerusalem; for then the re-establishment of the theocracy began, namely, at the return of Ezra to Jerusalem, 457 B.C. So Jeremiah's seventy years of the captivity begin 606 B.C., eighteen years before the destruction of Jerusalem, for then Judah ceased to exist as an independent theocracy, having fallen under the sway of Babylon. Two periods are marked in Ezra: (1) The return from the captivity under Jeshua and Zerubbabel, and rebuilding of the temple, which was the first anxiety of the theocratic nation. (2) The return of Ezra (regarded by the Jews as a second Moses) from Persia to Jerusalem, the restoration of the city, the nationality, and the law. Artaxerxes, in the seventh year of his reign, gave him the commission which virtually includes permission to rebuild the city, afterwards confirmed to, and carried out by, Nehemiah in the twentieth year (<reference osisRef="Ezra.9.9">Ezr 9:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezra.7.11">7:11</reference>, &c.). <reference osisRef="Dan.9.25">Da 9:25</reference>, "from the going forth of the commandment to build Jerusalem," proves that the second of the two periods is referred to. The words in <reference osisRef="Dan.9.24">Da 9:24</reference> are not, "are determined upon the holy city," but "upon thy people and thy holy city"; thus the restoration of the religious national polity and the law (the inner work fulfilled by Ezra the priest), and the rebuilding of the houses and walls (the outer work of Nehemiah, the governor), are both included in <reference osisRef="Dan.9.25">Da 9:25</reference>, "restore and build Jerusalem." "Jerusalem" represents both the city, the body, and the congregation, the soul of the state. Compare Psa 46:1-11; 48:1-14; 87:1-7. The starting-point of the seventy weeks dated from eighty-one years after Daniel received the prophecy: the object being not to fix for him definitely the time, but for the Church: the prophecy taught him that the Messianic redemption, which he thought near, was separated from him by at least a half millennium. Expectation was sufficiently kept alive by the general conception of the time; not only the Jews, but many Gentiles looked for some great Lord of the earth to spring from Judea at that very time [Tacitus, Histories, 5.13; Suetonius, Vespasian, 4]. Ezra's placing of Daniel in the canon immediately before his own book and Nehemiah's was perhaps owing to his feeling that he himself brought about the beginning of the fulfilment of the prophecy (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.20-Dan.9.27">Da 9:20-27</reference>) [Auberlen].<div eID="gen22030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22031" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">determined--</hi>literally, "cut out," namely, from the whole course of time, for God to deal in a particular manner with Jerusalem.<div eID="gen22031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22032" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy ... thy--</hi>Daniel had in his prayer often spoken of Israel as "Thy people, Thy holy city"; but Gabriel, in reply, speaks of them as Daniel's ("thy ... thy") people and city, God thus intimating that until the "everlasting righteousness" should be brought in by Messiah, He could not fully own them as His [Tregelles] (compare <reference osisRef="Exod.32.7">Ex 32:7</reference>). Rather, as God is wishing to console Daniel and the godly Jews, "the people whom thou art so anxiously praying for"; such weight does God give to the intercessions of the righteous (<reference osisRef="Jas.5.16-Jas.5.18">Jas 5:16-18</reference>).<div eID="gen22032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22033" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">finish--</hi>literally, "shut up"; remove from God's sight, that is, abolish (<reference osisRef="Ps.51.9">Psa 51:9</reference>) [Lengkerke]. The seventy years' exile was a punishment, but not a full atonement, for the sin of the people; this would come only after seventy prophetic weeks, through Messiah.<div eID="gen22033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22034" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">make an end of--</hi>The Hebrew reading, "to steal," that is, to hide out of sight (from the custom of sealing up things to be concealed, compare <reference osisRef="Job.9.7">Job 9:7</reference>), is better supported.<div eID="gen22034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22035" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">make reconciliation for--</hi>literally, "to cover," to overlay (as with pitch, <reference osisRef="Gen.6.14">Ge 6:14</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.32.1">Psa 32:1</reference>.<div eID="gen22035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22036" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bring in everlasting righteousness--</hi>namely, the restoration of the normal state between God and man (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.5">Jr 23:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.23.6">6</reference>); to continue eternally (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.12">He 9:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.14.6">Re 14:6</reference>).<div eID="gen22036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22037" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seal up ... vision ... prophecy--</hi>literally, "prophet." To give the seal of confirmation to the prophet and his vision by the fulfilment.<div eID="gen22037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22038" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">anoint the Most Holy--</hi>primarily, to "anoint," or to consecrate after its pollution "the Most Holy" place but mainly Messiah, the antitype to the Most Holy place (<reference osisRef="John.2.19-John.2.22">Joh 2:19-22</reference>). The propitiatory in the temple (the same Greek word expresses the mercy seat and propitiation, <reference osisRef="Rom.3.25">Ro 3:25</reference>), which the Jews looked for at the restoration from Babylon, shall have its true realization only in Messiah. For it is only when sin is "made an end of" that God's presence can be perfectly manifested. As to "anoint," compare <reference osisRef="Exod.40.9">Ex 40:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.40.34">34</reference>. Messiah was anointed with the Holy Ghost (<reference osisRef="Acts.4.27">Ac 4:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.10.38">10:38</reference>). So hereafter, God-Messiah will "anoint" or consecrate with His presence the holy place at Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.16">Jr 3:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.3.17">17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.27">Eze 37:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.28">28</reference>), after its pollution by Antichrist, of which the feast of dedication after the pollution by Antiochus was a type. <div eID="gen22038" type="x-p"/>
entries.983c6ea736220fdd0f3a5de1f989c831cb66230f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12160"/><div sID="gen22039" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12160"/><hi type="bold">25. from the going forth of the commandment--</hi>namely the command from God, whence originated the command of the Persian king (<reference osisRef="Ezra.6.14">Ezr 6:14</reference>). Auberlen remarks, there is but one Apocalypse in each Testament. Its purpose in each is to sum up all the preceding prophecies, previous to the "troublous times" of the Gentiles, in which there was to be no revelation. Daniel sums up all the previous Messianic prophecy, separating into its individual phases what the prophets had seen in one and the same perspective, the temporary deliverance from captivity and the antitypical final Messianic deliverance. The seventy weeks are separated (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.25-Dan.9.27">Da 9:25-27</reference>) into three unequal parts, seven, sixty-two, one. The seventieth is the consummation of the preceding ones, as the Sabbath of God succeeds the working days; an idea suggested by the division into weeks. In the sixty-nine weeks Jerusalem is restored, and so a place is prepared for Messiah wherein to accomplish His sabbatic work (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.25">Da 9:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.9.26">26</reference>) of "confirming the covenant" (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.27">Da 9:27</reference>). The Messianic time is the Sabbath of Israel's history, in which it had the offer of all God's mercies, but in which it was cut off for a time by its rejection of them. As the seventy weeks end with seven years, or a week, so they begin with seven times seven, that is, seven weeks. As the seventieth week is separated from the rest as a period of revelation, so it may be with the seven weeks. The number seven is associated with revelation; for the seven spirits of God are the mediators of all His revelations (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.4">Re 1:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.1">3:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.5">4:5</reference>). Ten is the number of what is human; for example, the world power issues in ten heads and ten horns (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.42">Da 2:42</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.7">7:7</reference>). Seventy is ten multiplied by seven, the human moulded by the divine. The seventy years of exile symbolize the triumph of the world power over Israel. In the seven times seventy years the world number ten is likewise contained, that is, God's people is still under the power of the world ("troublous times"); but the number of the divine is multiplied by itself; seven times seven years, at the beginning a period of Old Testament revelation to God's people by Ezra, Nehemiah, and Malachi, whose labors extend over about half a century, or seven weeks, and whose writings are last in the canon; and in the end, seven years, the period of New Testament revelation in Messiah. The commencing seven weeks of years of Old Testament revelation are hurried over, in order that the chief stress might rest on the Messianic week. Yet the seven weeks of Old Testament revelation are marked by their separation from the sixty-two, to be above those sixty-two wherein there was to be none.<div eID="gen22039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22040" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Messiah the Prince--</hi>Hebrew, Nagid. Messiah is Jesus' title in respect to Israel (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.2">Psa 2:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.27.37">Mt 27:37</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.27.42">42</reference>). Nagid, as Prince of the Gentiles (<reference osisRef="Isa.55.4">Is 55:4</reference>). Nagid is applied to Titus, only as representative of Christ, who designates the Roman destruction of Jerusalem as, in a sense, His coming (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.29-Matt.24.31">Mt 24:29-31</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.21.22">Joh 21:22</reference>). Messiah denotes His calling; Nagid, His power. He is to "be cut off, and there shall be nothing for Him." (So the Hebrew for "not for Himself," <reference osisRef="Dan.9.26">Da 9:26</reference>, ought to be translated). Yet He is "the Prince" who is to "come," by His representative at first, to inflict judgment, and at last in person.<div eID="gen22040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22041" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wall--</hi>the "trench" or "scarped rampart" [Tregelles]. The street and trench include the complete restoration of the city externally and internally, which was during the sixty-nine weeks. <div eID="gen22041" type="x-p"/>
entries.df0eac8015b14db7b389fe6630df96e35a8e033c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12161"/><div sID="gen22042" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12161"/><hi type="bold">26. after threescore and two weeks--</hi>rather, the threescore and two weeks. In this verse, and in <reference osisRef="Dan.9.27">Da 9:27</reference>, Messiah is made the prominent subject, while the fate of the city and sanctuary are secondary, being mentioned only in the second halves of the verses. Messiah appears in a twofold aspect, salvation to believers, judgment on unbelievers (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.34">Lu 2:34</reference>; compare Mal 3:1-6; 4:1-3). He repeatedly, in Passion week, connects His being "cut off" with the destruction of the city, as cause and effect (Mt 21:37-41; 23:37, 38; Lu 21:20-24; 23:<reference osisRef="Luke.24.28-Luke.24.31">28-31</reference>). Israel might naturally expect Messiah's kingdom of glory, if not after the seventy years' captivity, at least at the end of the sixty-two weeks; but, instead of that, shall be His death, and the consequent destruction of Jerusalem.<div eID="gen22042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22043" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not for himself--</hi>rather, "there shall be nothing to Him" [Hengstenberg]; not that the real object of His first coming (His spiritual kingdom) should be frustrated; but the earthly kingdom anticipated by the Jews should, for the present, come to naught, and not then be realized. Tregelles refers the title, "the Prince" (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.25">Da 9:25</reference>), to the time of His entering Jerusalem on an ass's colt, His only appearance as a king, and six days afterwards put to death as "King of the Jews."<div eID="gen22043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22044" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the people of the prince--</hi>the Romans, led by Titus, the representative of the world power, ultimately to be transferred to Messiah, and so called by Messiah's title, "the Prince"; as also because sent by Him, as His instrument of judgment (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.7">Mt 22:7</reference>).<div eID="gen22044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22045" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">end thereof--</hi>of the sanctuary. Tregelles takes it, "the end of the Prince," the last head of the Roman power, Antichrist.<div eID="gen22045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22046" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with a flood--</hi>namely, of war (<reference osisRef="Ps.90.5">Psa 90:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.8.7">Is 8:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.8.8">8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.28.18">28:18</reference>). Implying the completeness of the catastrophe, "not one stone left on another."<div eID="gen22046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22047" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto the end of the war--</hi>rather, "unto the end there is war."<div eID="gen22047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22048" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">determined--</hi>by God's decree (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.23">Is 10:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.28.22">28:22</reference>). <div eID="gen22048" type="x-p"/>
entries.5fa8dbdfd46031bd628a55061005a3d6667a3fa5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12162"/><div sID="gen22049" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12162"/><hi type="bold">27. he shall confirm the covenant--</hi>Christ. The confirmation of the covenant is assigned to Him also elsewhere. <reference osisRef="Isa.42.6">Is 42:6</reference>, "I will give thee for a covenant of the people" (that is, He in whom the covenant between Israel and God is personally expressed); compare <reference osisRef="Luke.22.20">Lu 22:20</reference>, "The new testament in My blood"; Mal 3:1, "the angel of the covenant"; <reference osisRef="Jer.31.31-Jer.31.34">Jr 31:31-34</reference>, describes the Messianic covenant in full. Contrast <reference osisRef="Dan.11.30">Da 11:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.32">32</reference>, "forsake the covenant," "do wickedly against the covenant." The prophecy as to Messiah's confirming the covenant with many would comfort the faithful in Antiochus' times, who suffered partly from persecuting enemies, partly from false friends (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.33-Dan.11.35">Da 11:33-35</reference>). Hence arises the similarity of the language here and in <reference osisRef="Dan.11.30">Da 11:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.32">32</reference>, referring to Antiochus, the type of Antichrist.<div eID="gen22049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22050" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with many--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.53.11">Is 53:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.20.28">Mt 20:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.26.28">26:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.5.15">Ro 5:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.5.19">19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.9.28">He 9:28</reference>).<div eID="gen22050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22051" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in ... midst of ... week--</hi>The seventy weeks extend to A.D. 33. Israel was not actually destroyed till A.D. 79, but it was so virtually, A.D. 33, about three or four years after Christ's death, during which the Gospel was preached exclusively to the Jews. When the Jews persecuted the Church and stoned Stephen (<reference osisRef="Acts.7.54-Acts.7.60">Ac 7:54-60</reference>), the respite of grace granted to them was at an end (<reference osisRef="Luke.13.7-Luke.13.9">Lu 13:7-9</reference>). Israel, having rejected Christ, was rejected by Christ, and henceforth is counted dead (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.2.17">Ge 2:17</reference> with <reference osisRef="Gen.5.5">Ge 5:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.13.1">Ho 13:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.13.2">2</reference>), its actual destruction by Titus being the consummation of the removal of the kingdom of God from Israel to the Gentiles (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.43">Mt 21:43</reference>), which is not to be restored until Christ's second coming, when Israel shall be at the head of humanity (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.39">Mt 23:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.1.6">Ac 1:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.7">7</reference>; Ro 11:25-31; 15:1-32). The interval forms for the covenant-people a great parenthesis.<div eID="gen22051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22052" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he shall cause the sacrifice ... oblation to cease--</hi>distinct from the temporary "taking away" of "the daily" (sacrifice) by Antiochus (<reference osisRef="Dan.8.11">Da 8:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.11.31">11:31</reference>). Messiah was to cause all sacrifices and oblations in general to "cease" utterly. There is here an allusion only to Antiochus' act; to comfort God's people when sacrificial worship was to be trodden down, by pointing them to the Messianic time when salvation would fully come and yet temple sacrifices cease. This is the same consolation as Jeremiah and Ezekiel gave under like circumstances, when the destruction of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar was impending (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.16">Jr 3:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.31.31">31:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.11.19">Eze 11:19</reference>). Jesus died in the middle of the last week, A.D. 30. His prophetic life lasted three and a half years; the very time in which "the saints are given into the hand" of Antichrist (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.25">Da 7:25</reference>). Three and a half does not, like ten, designate the power of the world in its fulness, but (while opposed to the divine, expressed by seven) broken and defeated in its seeming triumph; for immediately after the three and a half times, judgment falls on the victorious world powers (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.25">Da 7:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.26">26</reference>). So Jesus' death seemed the triumph of the world, but was really its defeat (<reference osisRef="John.12.31">Joh 12:31</reference>). The rending of the veil marked the cessation of sacrifices through Christ's death (<reference osisRef="Lev.4.6">Le 4:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.17">17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.16.2">16:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.16.15">15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.14-Heb.10.18">He 10:14-18</reference>). There cannot be a covenant without sacrifice (<reference osisRef="Gen.8.20">Ge 8:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.9.17">9:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.15.9">15:9</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="Heb.9.15">He 9:15</reference>). Here the old covenant is to be confirmed, but in a way peculiar to the New Testament, namely, by the one sacrifice, which would terminate all sacrifices (<reference osisRef="Ps.40.6">Psa 40:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.40.11">11</reference>). Thus as the Levitical rites approached their end, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel, with ever increasing clearness, oppose the spiritual new covenant to the transient earthly elements of the old.<div eID="gen22052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22053" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for the overspreading of abominations--</hi>On account of the abominations committed by the unholy people against the Holy One, He shall not only destroy the city and sanctuary (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.25">Da 9:25</reference>), but shall continue its desolation until the time of the consummation "determined" by God (the phrase is quoted from <reference osisRef="Isa.10.22">Is 10:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.23">23</reference>), when at last the world power shall be judged and dominion be given to the saints of the Most High (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.26">Da 7:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.27">27</reference>). Auberlen translates, "On account of the desolating summit of abominations (compare <reference osisRef="Dan.11.31">Da 11:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.12.11">12:11</reference>; thus the repetition of the same thing as in <reference osisRef="Dan.9.26">Da 9:26</reference> is avoided), and till the consummation which is determined, it (the curse, <reference osisRef="Dan.9.11">Da 9:11</reference>, foretold by Moses) will pour on the desolated." Israel reached the summit of abominations, which drew down desolation (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.28">Mt 24:28</reference>), nay, which is the desolation itself, when, after murdering Messiah, they offered sacrifices, Mosaic indeed in form, but heathenish in spirit (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.1.13">Is 1:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.11">Eze 5:11</reference>). Christ refers to this passage (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.15">Mt 24:15</reference>), "When ye see the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel the prophet, stand in the holy place" (the latter words being tacitly implied in "abominations" as being such as are committed against the sanctuary). Tregelles translates, "upon the wing of abominations shall be that which causeth desolation"; namely, an idol set up on a wing or pinnacle of the temple (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.4.5">Mt 4:5</reference>) by Antichrist, who makes a covenant with the restored Jews for the last of the seventy weeks of years (fulfilling Jesus' words, "If another shall come in his own name, him ye will receive"), and for the first three and a half years keeps it, then in the midst of the week breaks it, causing the daily sacrifices to cease. Tregelles thus identifies the last half week with the time, times, and a half of the persecuting little horn (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.25">Da 7:25</reference>). But thus there is a gap of at least 1830 years put between the sixty-nine weeks and the seventieth week. Sir Isaac Newton explains the wing ("overspreading") of abominations to be the Roman ensigns (eagles) brought to the east gate of the temple, and there sacrificed to by the soldiers; the war, ending in the destruction of Jerusalem, lasted from spring A.D. 67 to autumn A.D. 70, that is, just three and a half years, or the last half week of years [Josephus, Wars of the Jews, 6.6].<div eID="gen22053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22054" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">poured upon the desolate--</hi>Tregelles translates, "the causer of desolation," namely, Antichrist. Compare "abomination that maketh desolate" (<reference osisRef="Dan.12.11">Da 12:11</reference>). Perhaps both interpretations of the whole passage may be in part true; the Roman desolator, Titus, being a type of Antichrist, the final desolator of Jerusalem. Bacon [The Advancement of Learning, 2.3] says, "Prophecies are of the nature of the Author, with whom a thousand years are as one day; and therefore are not fulfilled punctually at once, but have a springing and germinant accomplishment through many years, though the height and fulness of them may refer to one age." <chapter eID="Dan.9"/>

entries.a57dedde3fbbd8269befdaea4b4343ebbd79dfe1: <div eID="gen33222" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen33223" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33224" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33224" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33223" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33225" type="x-p"/> Daniel, understanding from the prophecies of Jeremiah that the seventy years' captivity was now terminating, pours out his soul in fervent prayer to God, and earnestly supplicates pardon and restoration for his captive people, <reference osisRef="Dan.9.1-Dan.9.12">Dan 9:1-12</reference>. When thus supplicating God in behalf of Israel, the angel Gabriel is sent to inform him of the seventy prophetic weeks, or four hundred and ninety natural years, which should elapse from the date of the edict to rebuild Jerusalem and the temple to the death of the Messiah, <reference osisRef="Dan.9.20-Dan.9.27">Dan 9:20-27</reference>; a prophecy most exactly fulfilled by the event, according to the computation of the best chronologers. Dean Prideaux states the commencement of these seventy prophetic weeks to have been in the month Nisan, in the year of the Julian period 4256, which corresponds with A.M. 3546, b.c. 458, according to the Usherian account. How awfully are the Jews blinded, who, in contradiction to so clear a prophecy, still expect the Messiah who was cut off, and, after suffering, is entered into his glory! <div eID="gen33225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33226" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen33226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33227" type="x-p"/> In the first year on Darius - This is the same Darius the Mede, spoken of before, who succeeded Belshazzar, king of the Chaldeans. See <reference osisRef="Dan.5.31">Dan 5:31</reference>.
entries.a471fd32ff4e691a5623d904c84cae02d016176e: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen33227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33228" type="x-p"/> I Daniel understood by books - The prophecy referred to here is found <reference osisRef="Jer.25.12">Jer 25:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.29.10">Jer 29:10</reference>. The people must have been satisfied of the Divine inspiration of Jeremiah, or his prophecies would not have been so speedily collected nor so carefully preserved. It appears that there was a copy of them then in Daniel's hands.
entries.b8866da560bc84053781388b2c5d99f4b7fd7527: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen33228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33229" type="x-p"/> I set my face - to seek by prayer - He found that the time of the promised deliverance could not be at any great distance; and as he saw nothing that indicated a speedy termination of their oppressive captivity, he was very much afflicted, and earnestly besought God to put a speedy end to it; and how earnestly he seeks, his own words show. He prayed, he supplicated, he fasted, he put sackcloth upon his body, and he put ashes upon his head. He uses that kind of prayer prescribed by Solomon in his prayer at the dedication of the temple. See <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.47">1Kgs 8:47</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.48">1Kgs 8:48</reference>.
entries.78f3dc45c3b29942a287bb6cda1e289126d42e18: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen33229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33230" type="x-p"/> Keeping the covenant - Fidelity and truth are characteristics of God. He had never yet broken his engagements to his followers, and was ever showing mercy to men.
entries.8dddf16313ac37270ee28ef2a9b6d2d12d26ca3b: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen33230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33231" type="x-p"/> All Israel, that are near, and that are far off - He prays both for Judah and Israel. The latter were more dispersed, and had been much longer in captivity.
entries.fc38f1481b4722b541d6c3f09c76be056d0e55af: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen33231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33232" type="x-p"/> Mercies and forgivenesses - From God's goodness flow God's mercies; from his mercies, forgivenesses.
entries.1ee88d56ca3cdfbcfebf8b8a88685edc158cf176: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen33232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33233" type="x-p"/> Therefore the curse is poured upon us - It is probable that he alludes here to the punishment of certain criminals by pouring melted metal upon them; therefore he uses the word תתך tittach. it is poured out, like melted metal, for this is the proper meaning of the root נתך nathach.
entries.706e371412c312d34356e9a05efd36da1a7c3cdc: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen33233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33234" type="x-p"/> The Lord watched upon the evil - In consequence of our manifold rebellions he hath now watched for an opportunity to bring these calamities upon us.
entries.03e49d14e2565f0c6854ecd5a00f238da4bd7deb: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen33234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33235" type="x-p"/> And cause thy face to shine - Give us proof that thou art reconciled to us.
entries.a8c268148bf601ce5fc8edee93b4b3693bb2d3ed: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen33235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33236" type="x-p"/> Thy city and thy people are called by thy name - The holy city, the city of the great King. I think it scarcely possible for any serious man to read these impressive and pleading words without feeling a measure of the prophet's earnestness.
entries.8f8c8c75f4cbc8048757f73d249a21eee23d7ed7: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen33236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33237" type="x-p"/> The man Gabriel - Or the angel Gabriel, who had appeared to me as a man. איש ish is the same here as person - the person Gabriel. <div eID="gen33237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33238" type="x-p"/> Being caused to fly swiftly - God hears with delight such earnest, humble, urgent prayers; and sends the speediest answer. Gabriel himself was ordered on this occasion to make more than usual speed.
entries.5c1308f2fae837dc63f3ffa747ad527f87f01672: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen33238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33239" type="x-p"/> Seventy weeks are determined - This is a most important prophecy, and has given rise to a variety of opinions relative to the proper mode of explanation; but the chief difficulty, if not the only one, is to find out the time from which these seventy weeks should be dated. What is here said by the angel is not a direct answer to Daniel's prayer. He prays to know when the seventy weeks of the captivity are to end. Gabriel shows him that there are seventy weeks determined relative to a redemption from another sort of captivity, which shall commence with the going forth of the edict to restore and rebuild Jerusalem, and shall terminate with the death of Messiah the Prince, and the total abolition of the Jewish sacrifices. In the four following verses he enters into the particulars of this most important determination, and leaves them with Daniel for his comfort, who has left them to the Church of God for the confirmation of its faith, and a testimony to the truth of Divine revelation. They contain the fullest confirmation of Christianity, and a complete refutation of the Jewish cavils and blasphemies on this subject. <div eID="gen33239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33240" type="x-p"/> Of all the writers I have consulted on this most noble prophecy, Dean Prideaux appears to me the most clear and satisfactory. I shall therefore follow his method in my explanation, and often borrow his words. <div eID="gen33240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33241" type="x-p"/> Seventy weeks are determined - The Jews had Sabbatic years, <reference osisRef="Lev.25.8">Lev 25:8</reference>, by which their years were divided into weeks of years, as in this important prophecy, each week containing seven years. The seventy weeks therefore here spoken of amount to four hundred and ninety years. <div eID="gen33241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33242" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Dan.9.24">Dan 9:24</reference> there are six events mentioned which should be the consequences of the incarnation of our Lord: - <div eID="gen33242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33243" type="x-p"/> I. To finish (לכלא lechalle, to restrain), the transgression which was effected by the preaching of the Gospel, and pouring out of the Holy Ghost among men. <div eID="gen33243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33244" type="x-p"/> II. To make an end of sins; rather ולהתם חטאות ulehathem chataoth, "to make an end of sin-offerings," which our Lord did when he offered his spotless soul and body on the cross once for all. <div eID="gen33244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33245" type="x-p"/> III. To make reconciliation (ולכפר ulechapper, "to make atonement or expiation") for iniquity; which he did by the once offering up of himself. <div eID="gen33245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33246" type="x-p"/> IV. To bring in everlasting righteousness, צדק עלמים tsedek olamim, that is, "the righteousness, or righteous One, of ages;" that person who had been the object of the faith of mankind, and the subject of the predictions of the prophets through all the ages of the world. <div eID="gen33246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33247" type="x-p"/> V. To seal up (ולחתם velachtom, "to finish or complete") the vision and prophecy; that is, to put an end to the necessity of any farther revelations, by completing the canon of Scripture, and fulfilling the prophecies which related to his person, sacrifice, and the glory that should follow. <div eID="gen33247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33248" type="x-p"/> VI. And to anoint the Most Holy, קדש קדשים kodesh kodashim, "the Holy of holies." משיח mashach, to anoint, (from which comes משיח mashiach, the Messiah, the anointed one), signifies in general, to consecrate or appoint to some special office. Here it means the consecration or appointment of our blessed Lord, the Holy One of Israel, to be the Prophet, Priest, and King of mankind.
entries.e2a36dce7e7f13a666df6667041c92079c96d1cc: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen33248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33249" type="x-p"/> From the going forth of the commandment to restore and to build Jerusalem - The foregoing events being all accomplished by Jesus Christ, they of course determine the prophecy to him. And if we reckon back four hundred and ninety years, we shall find the time of the going forth of this command. <div eID="gen33249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33250" type="x-p"/> Most learned men agree that the death of Christ happened at the passover in the month Nisan, in the four thousand seven hundred and forty-sixth year of the Julian period. Four hundred and ninety years, reckoned back from the above year, leads us directly to the month Nisan in the four thousand two hundred and fifty-sixth year of the same period; the very month and year in which Ezra had his commission from Artaxerxes Longimanus, king of Persia, (see <reference osisRef="Ezr.7.9">Ezr 7:9</reference>), to restore and rebuild Jerusalem. See the commission in Ezra 7:11-26 (note), and Prideaux's Connexions, vol. 2 p. 380. <div eID="gen33250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33251" type="x-p"/> The above seventy weeks, or four hundred and ninety years, are divided, in <reference osisRef="Ezr.7.25">Ezr 7:25</reference>, into three distinct periods, to each of which particular events are assigned. The three periods are: - <div eID="gen33251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33252" type="x-p"/> I. Seven weeks, that is, forty-nine years. <div eID="gen33252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33253" type="x-p"/> II. Sixty-two weeks, that is, four hundred and thirty-four years. <div eID="gen33253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33254" type="x-p"/> III. One week, that is, seven years. <div eID="gen33254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33255" type="x-p"/> To the first period of seven weeks the restoration and repairing of Jerusalem are referred; and so long were Ezra and Nehemiah employed in restoring the sacred constitutions and civil establishments of the Jews, for this work lasted forty-nine years after the commission was given by Artaxerxes. <div eID="gen33255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33256" type="x-p"/> From the above seven weeks the second period of sixty-two weeks, or four hundred and thirty-four years more, commences, at the end of which the prophecy says, Messiah the Prince should come, that is, seven weeks, or forty-nine years, should be allowed for the restoration of the Jewish state; from which time till the public entrance of the Messiah on the work of the ministry should be sixty-two weeks, or four hundred and thirty-four years, in all four hundred and eighty-three years. <div eID="gen33256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33257" type="x-p"/> From the coming of our Lord, the third period is to be dated, viz., "He shall confirm the covenant with many for one week," that is seven years, <reference osisRef="Dan.9.27">Dan 9:27</reference>. <div eID="gen33257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33258" type="x-p"/> This confirmation of the covenant must take in the ministry of John the Baptist with that of our Lord, comprehending the term of seven years, during the whole of which he might be well said to confirm or ratify the new covenant with mankind. Our Lord says, "The law was until John;" but from his first public preaching the kingdom of God, or Gospel dispensation, commenced. <div eID="gen33258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33259" type="x-p"/> These seven years, added to the four hundred and eighty-three, complete the four hundred and ninety years, or seventy prophetic weeks; so that the whole of this prophecy, from the times and corresponding events, has been fulfilled to the very letter. <div eID="gen33259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33260" type="x-p"/> Some imagine that the half of the last seven years is to be referred to the total destruction of the Jews by Titus, when the daily sacrifice for ever ceased to be offered; and that the intermediate space of thirty-seven years, from our Lord's death till the destruction of the city, is passed over as being of no account in relation to the prophecy, and that it was on this account that the last seven years are divided. But Dean Prideaux thinks that the whole refers to our Lord's preaching connected with that of the Baptist. וחצי vachatsi, says he, signifies in the half part of the week; that is, in the latter three years and a half in which he exercised himself in the public ministry, he caused, by the sacrifice of himself, all other sacrifices and oblations to cease, which were instituted to signify his. <div eID="gen33260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33261" type="x-p"/> In the latter parts of <reference osisRef="Dan.9.26">Dan 9:26</reference> and <reference osisRef="Dan.9.27">Dan 9:27</reference> we find the Third Part of this great prophecy, which refers to what should be done after the completion of these seventy weeks.
entries.8550d908417f2beee3465c4f09b9ec99337bb0e8: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen33261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33262" type="x-p"/> And the people of the prince that shall come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary - By the "prince" Titus, the son of Vespasian, is plainly intended; and "the people of that prince" are no other than the Romans, who, according to the prophecy, destroyed the sanctuary, הקדש hakkodesh, the holy place or temple, and, as a flood, swept away all, till the total destruction of that obstinate people finished the war.
entries.7abff3e058f55eac832b8e15f470ad58b7eee072: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen33262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33263" type="x-p"/> And for the overspreading of abominations he shall make it desolate - This clause is remarkably obscure. כנף שקוצים משמם kenaph shikkutsim meshomem, "And upon the wing of abominations causing amazement." This is a literal translation of the place; but still there is no determinate sense. A Hebrews MS., written in the thirteenth century, has preserved a very remarkable reading here, which frees the place from all embarrassment. Instead of the above reading, this valuable MS. has ובהיכל יהיה שיקוץ ubeheychal yihyey shikkuts; that is, "And in the temple (of the Lord) there shall be abomination." This makes the passage plain, and is strictly conformable to the facts themselves, for the temple was profaned; and it agrees with the prediction of our Lord, who said that the abomination that maketh desolate should stand in the holy place, <reference osisRef="Mat.24.15">Mat 24:15</reference>, and quotes the words as spoken δια Δανιηλ του φροφητου, by Daniel the prophet. That the above reading gives the true sense, there can be little doubt, because it is countenanced by the most eminent ancient versions. <div eID="gen33263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33264" type="x-p"/> The Vulgate reads, Et erit in templo abominatio, "And in the temple there shall be abomination." <div eID="gen33264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33265" type="x-p"/> The Septuagint, Και επι το ἱερον βδελυγμα των ερημωσεων, "And upon the temple there shall be the abomination of desolation." <div eID="gen33265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33266" type="x-p"/> The Arabic, "And upon the sanctuary there shall be the abomination of ruin." <div eID="gen33266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33267" type="x-p"/> The above reading is celebrated by J. D. Michaelis, Epist. De Ebdom. Dan., p. 120: Vix insignius exemplum reperiri posse autumem, ostensuro in codicibus Hebraeis latere lectiones dignissimas quae eruantur, etc. "A more illustrious example can, I think, hardly be found, to show that various readings lie hid in Hebrew MSS., which are most worthy of being exhibited." Vid. Bib. Hebrews Kennicott, Dis. Gen. <div eID="gen33267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33268" type="x-p"/> I have only to add that this mode of reckoning years and periods by weeks is not solely Jewish. Macrobius, in his book on Scipio's dream, has these remarkable words: Sed a sexta usque ad septimam septimanam fit quidem diminutio, sed occulta, et quae detrimentum suum aperta defectione non prodat: ideo nonnullarum rerumpublicarum hic mos est, ut post sextam ad militiam nemo cogatur; Somn. Scip., lib. 1 c. vi., in fine. "From the sixth to the seventh week, there is a diminution of strength; but it is hidden, and does not manifest itself by any outward defect. Hence it was the custom in some republics not to oblige a man to go to the wars after the sixth week, i.e., after forty-two years of age." <div eID="gen33268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33269" type="x-p"/> Various Readings of <reference osisRef="Dan.9.24-Dan.9.27">Dan 9:24-27</reference> <div eID="gen33269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33270" type="x-p"/> Having now gone through the whole of this important prophecy, and given that interpretation which the original seemed best to warrant, I shall next proceed to notice the principal various readings found in the Collections of Kennicott and De Rossi, with those from my own MSS., which the reader may collate with the words of the common printed text. <reference osisRef="Dan.9.24">Dan 9:24</reference> שבעים שבעים נחתך על עמך ועל עיר קדשך לכלא הפשע ולחתם חטאות ולכפר עו ולהביא צדק עלמים ובצלחתם חזו ונביא ולמשח קדש קדשים׃ <reference osisRef="Dan.9.25">Dan 9:25</reference> ותדע ותשכל מן מצא דבר להשיב ולבנות ירושלם עד משיח נגיד שבעים שבעה ושבעים ששים ושנים תשוב ונבנתה רחוב וחרוץ ובצוק העתים׃ <reference osisRef="Dan.9.26">Dan 9:26</reference> ואחרי השבעים ששים ושנים יכרת משיח ואין לו והעיר והקדש ישחית עם נגיד הבא וקצו בשטף ועד קץ מלחמה נחרצת שממות׃ <reference osisRef="Dan.9.27">Dan 9:27</reference> והגביר ברית לרבים שבוע אחד וחצי השבוע ישבית זבח ומנחה ועל כנף שקוצים משמם ועד כלה ונחרצה תתך על שומם׃ <div eID="gen33270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33271" type="x-p"/> Houbigant's Translation of <reference osisRef="Dan.9.24-Dan.9.27">Dan 9:24-27</reference> <div eID="gen33271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33272" type="x-p"/> Of the whole passage Houbigant gives the following translation: - <reference osisRef="Dan.9.24">Dan 9:24</reference> <div eID="gen33272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33273" type="x-p"/> Seventy weeks are determined upon thy people, and the city of thy sanctuary: <div eID="gen33273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33274" type="x-p"/> That sin may be restrained, and transgressions have an end; <div eID="gen33274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33275" type="x-p"/> That iniquity may be expiated, and an everlasting righteousness brought in; <div eID="gen33275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33276" type="x-p"/> That visions and prophecies may be sealed up, and the Holy of holies anointed. <reference osisRef="Dan.9.25">Dan 9:25</reference> <div eID="gen33276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33277" type="x-p"/> Know therefore and understand: - <div eID="gen33277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33278" type="x-p"/> From the edict which shall be promulgated, to return and rebuild Jerusalem, there shall be seven weeks. <div eID="gen33278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33279" type="x-p"/> Then it shall be fully rebuilt, with anxiety, in difficult times. <div eID="gen33279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33280" type="x-p"/> Thence, to the Prince Messiah, there shall be sixty-two weeks. <reference osisRef="Dan.9.26">Dan 9:26</reference> <div eID="gen33280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33281" type="x-p"/> And after sixty-two weeks the Messiah shall be slain, and have no justice. <div eID="gen33281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33282" type="x-p"/> Afterwards he shall waste the city and the sanctuary, by the prince that is to come. <div eID="gen33282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33283" type="x-p"/> And his end shall be in straits; and to the end of the war desolation is appointed. <reference osisRef="Dan.9.27">Dan 9:27</reference> <div eID="gen33283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33284" type="x-p"/> And for one week he shall confirm a covenant with many; <div eID="gen33284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33285" type="x-p"/> And in the middle of the week he shall abrogate sacrifice and offering; And in the temple there shall be the abomination of desolation, <div eID="gen33285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33286" type="x-p"/> Until the ruin which is decreed rush on after the desolation. <div eID="gen33286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33287" type="x-p"/> In this translation there are some peculiarities. <div eID="gen33287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33288" type="x-p"/> Instead of "the street shall be built again, and the wall," <reference osisRef="Dan.9.26">Dan 9:26</reference>, he translates רחוב וחרוץ (with the prefix ב beth instead of ו vau in the latter word), "it shall be fully (the city and all its walls) rebuilt with anxiety." <div eID="gen33288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33289" type="x-p"/> Instead of ואי לו "but not for himself," he translates, "Nor shall justice be done him;" supposing that די "justice" was originally in the verse. <div eID="gen33289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33290" type="x-p"/> Instead of "the people of the prince," <reference osisRef="Dan.9.26">Dan 9:26</reference>, he translates "by the prince," using עם im as a preposition, instead of עם am, "the people." <div eID="gen33290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33291" type="x-p"/> Instead of "and for the overspreading," he translates ועל כנף "in the temple;" following the Septuagint, και επι το ἱερον. This rendering is at least as good as ours: but see the marginal readings here, and the preceding notes. <div eID="gen33291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33292" type="x-p"/> Houbigant contends also that the arrangement of the several members in these passages is confused. He proposes one alteration, which is important, viz., From the promulgation of the decree to rebuild Jerusalem shall be seven weeks; and unto Messiah the prince, sixty-two weeks. All these alterations he vindicates in his notes at the end of this chapter. In the text I have inserted Houbigant's dots, or marks of distinction between the different members of the verses. <div eID="gen33292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33293" type="x-p"/> Various Readings <reference osisRef="Dan.9.24">Dan 9:24</reference> שבוים שבעים weeks written full, so to prevent mistakes, in thirteen of Kennicott's, four of De Rossi's, and one ancient of my own. שבעים Seventy-one of Kennicott's, and one of De Rossi's, have שבועים "weeks, weeks, weeks;" that is, "many weeks:" but this is a mere mistake. לכלא "to restrain." לכלח "to consume," is the reading of twenty-nine of Kennicott's, thirteen of De Rossi's, and one ancient of my own. ולחתם "and to seal up." Forty-three of Kennicott's, twelve of De Rossi's, and one of my own, have ולחתם "to make an end." One reads ולחתום, more full. חטאות "sins." חטאת "sin," in the singular, is the reading of twenty-six of De Rossi's; and so, in the second instance where this word occurs, two of my MSS. עלמים "everlasting." Two of my oldest MSS read שלמים, and so in the next instance. ונביא "and the prophet." The conjunction is omitted by two of Kennicott's. ותשכל "and understand." One of my MSS. has ותשכיל. <reference osisRef="Dan.9.25">Dan 9:25</reference> מן מוצא "from the publication." One MS. of De Rossi's omits the מן "from," and instead of either, one of my oldest MSS. has למוצא "to the publication." משיה "Messiah." Nine MSS. read the word with the point sheva, which makes it read, in regimine, "the anointed of the prince." But this is evidently the effect of carelessness, or rather design. שבעה "seven." Two MSS. add the conjunction ו vau, "and." ולבנות "and to build." One of mine omits the conjunction. שבעים שבעה "seven weeks." One of Kennicott's has שבעים שבה "seventy years." ושבעים "and weeks." One of Kennicott's has ושבוע and a week." ששים "sixty." A few add the conjunction ו vau, "and sixty;" and another has ששה "six;" and another שבעים "seventy." Wherever this word signifies weeks, two of my oldest MSS. write it full שבועים. In one of my MSS. השבועים ששים are omitted in the text, but added by a later hand in the margin. וחרוץ "and the ditch." One MS. has העיר "the city." And for רחב "street," one of mine has רחוב of the same meaning, but more full. ובצוק "and in straits," or anxiety. One MS. without and, as the Vulgate and Septuagint. <reference osisRef="Dan.9.26">Dan 9:26</reference> והקדש "and the holy place or sanctuary." But two of my most ancient MSS., and four of Kennicott's, leave out the ו vau, and read הקדש והעיר "and the holy city," or "city of holiness," instead of "the city and sanctuary." In one MS. ו is omitted in והעיר. וקצו "and its end." One MS. omits the conjunction ו and; one omits the following קץ "the end;" reading thus:" and unto the war." But a more singular reading is that of one of my own MSS. written about a.d. 1136, which has וקיצו "and its summer." ששים "sixty." But one of Kennicott's MSS. has ששים שבעים "sixty weeks;" and another adds the conjunction, And sixty. ישחית shall destroy." But one of De Rossi's has ישחת "shall be destroyed." עם "the people." עם im, "with," is the reading of one of Kennicott's, with the Septuagint, Theodotion, Syriac, Hexapla, Vulgate, and Arabic. בשטף "with a flood." One MS. has השטף "the flood." ועל כנף "and upon the wing." Nearly twenty MSS. have ועד "and unto," etc. <reference osisRef="Dan.9.27">Dan 9:27</reference> ועד קץ "and unto the end." עד־ "to the end;" and one has ועל "and upon." קץ "the end." One has עת "the time;" and another both, עת קץ "the time of the end." ועל כנף שקוצים "and upon the wing (or battlement) abomination." Instead of this, one of the Parisian MSS. numbered three hundred and thirteen in Kennicott's, has ובהיכל יהיה שיקוץ "and in the temple there shall be abomination." See the preceding notes. This is a similar reading to Theodotion, the Vulgate, Septuagint, Syriac, Hexapla, and the Arabic; and is countenanced by our Lord, <reference osisRef="Mat.24.15">Mat 24:15</reference>. After all that has been said on this reading, (which may be genuine, but is less liable to suspicion, as the MS. appears to be the work of some Christian; it is written from the left to the right hand, and is accompanied by the Vulgate Latin), if this be an attempt to accommodate the Hebrew to the Vulgate, it should be stated that they who have examined this MS. closely, have asserted that there is no evidence that the writer has endeavored to conform the Hebrew to the Latin text, unless this be accounted such. The ancient versions give this reading great credit. שקוצים "abominations." One of mine has less fully שקצים. משמם "desolation." One of mine has more fully משימם. ועד "and unto," is wanting in one of mine; ועל "and upon" is the reading in one other. על שומם "until the desolation." שומם "the desolation." One of mine has שמם without the ו vau. על is wanting; but is added in the margin, by a later hand, in another of these ancient MSS. <div eID="gen33293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33294" type="x-p"/> I have thus set down almost all the variations mentioned by Kennicott and De Rossi, and those furnished by three ancient MSS. of my own, that the learned reader may avail himself of every help to examine thoroughly this important prophecy. Upwards of thirty various readings in the compass of four verses, and several of them of great moment.  <chapter eID="Dan.9"/> <div eID="gen33294" type="x-p"/>

entries.8bcbe0beeed29fc1c396ec91266a1a1d422b894d: <div eID="gen15854" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">The Seventy Weeks</title> <div sID="gen15855" type="x-p"/> In the first year of Darius the Median, Daniel, by a diligent study of the prophecies of Jeremiah as to the number of years during which Jerusalem must lie desolate (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.1">Dan 9:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.9.2">Dan 9:2</reference>), was led to pour forth a penitential prayer, in which he acknowledges the justice of the divine chastisement which hung over Israel on account of their sins, and entreats the mercy of God in behalf of his people (vv. 3-19).
